newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Demand rises at Brazil government wheat auctions.
newsitem.headline: Demand rises at Brazil government wheat auctions.

text.p: Demand has picked up at Brazilian government auctions of domestic wheat and the government is increasing the payment period from December 20th to ease conditions for millers, Brazilian bank officials said.
In all, 107,535 tonnes of wheat have been sold of the 900,000 tonnes offered since November, according to Banco do Brasil, which handles the auctions.
Of this total, 86,856 tonnes were sold in the last three auctions between December 10th and 17th. As of December 6th, only 20,679 tonnes had been placed.
Analysts and millers said excess red tape and distrust of the new system had been responsible for low demand during the early auctions.
Banco do Brasil said it would be increasing the payment period for the wheat auctions to 10 days from five as of December 20th in order to ease conditions for buyers.
"The auctions are going very well," Antenor Barros Leal, president of the Brazilian Association of Wheat Industries (Abitrigo), told Reuters.
"The (slowness at) the beginning was normal because you have the logistics and nobody trusted what the government was saying. This is a normal pace," he added.
In auctions millers bid for wheat not at an outright price but at a subsidy to the minimum price of 157 reais ($152).
The miller pays the government the minimum price minus the subsidy set at the auction while the government pays the farmer the full minimum price.
The advantage for the government is that it does not have to pay for the storage of wheat as in previous years, with the wheat passing directly from the farmer to the mill.
Banco do Brasil said the subsidy at Tuesday's auction was around 31 reais ($29.80), almost double the level ten days earlier.
Abitrigo's Leal suggested the subsidy was at the right level, given that millers demand was currently good at around 30 percent of the 100,000 tonnes offered in each auction so far.

Farmers have been warning the slow demand at the auctions may result in a drop in output next year as producers see lower than expected returns from the increased plantings in 1996. Independent consultants Safras e Mercado are already forecasting that low prices and the subsequent lack of liquidity may mean the 1997 harvest will fall to no more than two million tonnes after doubling to 3.13 million tonnes in 1996.
